sum.a: Four dilemmas, one budget — the planner's problem
credit: Research demo — INOCS (Inria) · EU SUM project · preliminary placeholder results
a.title: Where should the bikes live?
a.lede: Geneva wants shared bikes that work with its trams and buses, not against them. You have one map, one budget, and the same dilemmas as the city's planners.
a.map.alt: Map of the 1.5 km study area in central Geneva
a.d1.p: Many small stations put a bike near everyone — and run empty by 9am. A few big ones never run dry, but whole neighbourhoods walk. You can't fully have both.
a.d2.h: Where does the tram hand over?
a.d2.p: A shared bike is most useful at the end of a transit ride. Which stops earn a bigger transfer station with extra docks?
a.d3.p: By evening the bikes sit where people went — not where tomorrow starts. Trucks rebalance them overnight, and every run costs money.
a.d4.p: That's the budget of Geneva's reference plan. Spend a quarter of it? Nearly double it? Each answer builds a different city.
a.note: This demo runs on real Geneva data — {trips} observed bike trips (Jun–Dec 2024) and a year of public-transport ridership — and on a research optimisation model by INOCS (Inria) in the EU SUM project.

b.cta: You've seen where Geneva moves. Take the budget →
b.ins.mon.0: The city sleeps — almost nothing moves before 6h.
b.ins.mon.1: Morning rush: flows pour into Cornavin and Bel-Air. Bikes parked here tonight will be gone by 9h.
b.ins.mon.2: Midday hum — steadier, spread across the centre and the university.
b.ins.mon.3: The day's biggest peak, 17–18h: everyone heads home at once. Docks fill up fast downtown.
b.ins.mon.4: Evening wind-down along the lake and Plainpalais.
b.ins.sun.0: No morning peak on Sundays — the commute pattern simply isn't there.
b.ins.sun.1: A slow start: leisure trips build through the late morning.
b.ins.sun.2: Sunday peaks at 16–18h — lakeside and old-town leisure, not commuting.
b.ins.sun.3: A quiet evening. A network tuned only for Monday would waste money today.
c.title: Choose a strategy
c.bridge.mon: At 8h the trams pour into Cornavin; by 17–18h everyone heads home at once.
c.bridge.sun: You watched Sunday: no morning rush, a long leisure afternoon peaking at 16–18h.
c.bridge.tail: Three budgets, three philosophies for serving that pulse. The optimiser places the stations — you set the ambition.

scen.S1_essential.name: Essential network
scen.S1_essential.pitch: The city invests the bare minimum. Where do the few stations go, and who is left out?
scen.S1_essential.narrative: With a small budget, the optimisation model has to triage: it concentrates stations where demand and public-transport connections pay off most, leaving whole neighbourhoods uncovered. In the simulation, some riders find no station nearby, and stations run empty during the morning peak.
scen.S1_essential.expect.service: the lowest coverage and served-trip ratio of the three plans
scen.S1_essential.expect.economics: the smallest investment, but the best return per euro spent — the first euros are the most productive
scen.S2_balanced.name: Balanced network
scen.S2_balanced.pitch: The city funds a solid network — the reference plan studied for Geneva.
scen.S2_balanced.narrative: This is the configuration behind the published Geneva proof-of-concept — an 80 000 € budget, 2.5% of it for operations — with one change: the demand weights come from the real observed trip data instead of random draws, so the design targets the actual morning and evening peaks. Coverage is broad and most trips are served on a typical Monday.
scen.S2_balanced.expect.service: high coverage, with occasional empty or full stations at peak hours
scen.S2_balanced.expect.economics: the reference cost per served trip — the plan the other two are measured against
scen.S3_ambitious.name: Ambitious green transition
scen.S3_ambitious.pitch: The city goes all in: a bigger budget and double the operating budget. Is it worth it?
scen.S3_ambitious.narrative: Nearly every zone gets a station, and rebalancing keeps them stocked, so almost no rider is turned away — even under Sunday's leisure pattern. But the KPIs show diminishing returns: each extra euro buys fewer additional served trips than in S2, and the cost per served trip rises. The lesson: 'more' isn't automatically 'better spent' — and quantifying that trade-off is exactly what the optimisation model is for.
scen.S3_ambitious.expect.service: the highest coverage and availability, on both Monday and Sunday
scen.S3_ambitious.expect.economics: the largest investment and the highest cost per served trip — diminishing returns, made visible
prov.p1: The station layouts shown are placeholder results: a simple greedy heuristic stands in while the real optimisation runs (Gurobi solver) are being produced. The screens, KPIs and data pipeline are final — the demo will refresh automatically when solver results replace the placeholders.
prov.p2: Simulation KPIs (service, mobility, CO₂, economics) are computed by the real evaluation pipeline on these placeholder layouts, from observed Geneva data. Every figure is traceable: tap “how is this computed?” next to any headline.
